🛰️ Exploring Earth Beyond the Visible

We are a team of curious and passionate problem-solvers interested in Earth observation, remote sensing, GIS, satellite imagery, and artificial intelligence.

Our mission is to turn satellite data into meaningful insights and develop innovative solutions to real-world environmental challenges.

We believe great ideas come from collaboration, creativity, and diverse perspectives.

Let's explore Earth from space and build something meaningful together! 🚀
summary:
Mongolia faces hazards that build up slowly and strike different places: dzud (deep snow and cold after a dry summer, which killed 21.7% of the country's livestock in 2009/10), floods, wildfires and dust storms. Hazard Watch, by team Spy Kids, turns open Earth-observation data into two linked maps that detect the trends behind them.

The trend we found: since 2001, NASA MODIS shows summer pasture greening in 322 of 339 soums (+15% in the median soum), while the herd grazing it nearly doubled.

ZudRisk scores dzud risk for all 339 soums from snow depth and winter cold (ERA5-Land), summer pasture greenness (NASA MODIS NDVI) and grazing pressure (livestock census), each compared with that soum's own 2001–2020 normal. Tested against real losses, its ranking reached a Spearman correlation of 0.60 in the dzud winters fixed in advance (0.44 over all winters).

Mongolia Hazard Watch maps flood, wildfire, dust storm and dzud risk day by day since 2001 using NASA MODIS, VIIRS, HLS and GIBS imagery, and computes flood extent, burned area or dust conditions for any drawn area. Its flood and wildfire indices are still being calibrated against recorded events.

Both are open, bilingual and free: https://mongolia-risk.vercel.app
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Hazard Watch, by team Spy Kids, is two linked, open web maps that watch Mongolia's slow disasters from space.

ZudRisk (https://zudrisk.vercel.app) scores dzud risk for all 339 soums. Dzud is the winter disaster that killed 21.7% of Mongolia's livestock in 2009/10. The map covers 25 past winters (2000/01–2024/25), a monthly-updated outlook for the current winter, a 25-year trend of summer greenness, and the government's official dzud criteria (Resolution 286).

Mongolia Hazard Watch (https://sigma0sanaa.github.io/hazard/) maps flood, wildfire, dust storm and dzud risk day by day since 2001. Users draw any area to compute flood extent from Sentinel-1 radar, burned area from Sentinel-2, or dust conditions, then download the result as GeoTIFF, Shapefile, GeoJSON, KML or KMZ.


THE TREND WE FOUND

Since 2001, NASA MODIS NDVI shows summer pasture greening in 322 of 339 soums: +15% in the median soum, statistically significant (Mann-Kendall, p < 0.05) in 157. Only 17 soums browned, all in the far west, none significantly. Over the same years the herd grew 1.9 times in sheep units (NSO): more grass, but far more animals on it.

HOW IT WORKS

ZudRisk combines four signals per soum: snow depth and winter cold (ERA5-Land), summer pasture greenness (NASA MODIS NDVI) and grazing pressure (national livestock census over each soum's pasture area). Each signal becomes a z-score against that soum's own 2001–2020 normal, so the map shows how unusual a winter is, not only how harsh. The weights come from published research (Nandintsetseg et al. 2018) and were fixed before any test. The score is calibrated into the chance that 5% or more of the herd dies.

Hazard Watch computes its archive in Google Earth Engine and runs the drawn-area analysis live in the browser on open Sentinel imagery.

VALIDATION AND HONESTY

On the five dzud winters we fixed in advance its ranking reaches a Spearman correlation of 0.60 (n = 1,683 soum-winters), and 0.44 over every soum-winter 2011–2025 (n = 4,688). The outlook sharpens as winter comes: 0.23 in October, 0.50 in November, 0.64 by December.

Every new idea gets a written rule before it is run, and failed ideas are published too (iron dzud, herd composition, fitted weights).

Hazard Watch's flood and wildfire risk indices are still in development: their thresholds are not yet calibrated against recorded events. That is our next step.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Soum and aimag governors can see where to stock hay and fodder before the snow, and where floods and fires threaten. NEMA can see where to send support first. Aid agencies and researchers get open maps and GIS files without coding. Both sites are bilingual (Mongolian/English), free, and need no login.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, netCDF4) data pipelines; JavaScript, HTML and CSS static sites with Leaflet; Google Earth Engine; Microsoft Planetary Computer; GitHub Actions for automatic daily updates; GitHub Pages and Vercel for hosting.

CREATIVITY

Each soum is compared with its own normal, not with the whole country. Satellite trends, real losses and official government criteria sit on one map. Area analysis runs entirely in the browser, with no server.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honest uncertainty (no overfitting; limits stated on the site); open and reproducible data and code; bilingual access for Mongolian users; low cost (free hosting, open data); clear labelling that this is not an official warning.
